summary: Covers operational considerations for DNS with IPv6, including special IPv6 addresses, known implementation misbehavior, naming for services, resolver support, and updates to forward and reverse trees. It is aimed at people who already know IPv4 DNS. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A handy guide for people who know the phone book for old addresses, telling them what changes and what traps to avoid with the new longer ones.

questions: how to deploy dns for ipv6
subtitle: Practical guidance for deploying DNS in IPv6 networks, for operators experienced with IPv4.

tldr.problem: DNS works differently in IPv6 networks than in IPv4, and operators need guidance on special address types, known implementation bugs, service naming strategies, and resolver configuration to avoid operational problems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents observed misbehaviors, provides recommendations for naming services, guidance on when to add IPv6 records, best practices for DNS resolvers, and considerations for updating both forward and reverse DNS with IPv6.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can use this guide to successfully transition to IPv6 DNS, avoiding pitfalls like premature AAAA queries or incomplete AAAA records that degrade performance.

facts.label: Minimum DNS servers
facts.value: At least one IPv4-enabled per zone

today: RFC 4472 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary reference for operational guidance on deploying IPv6 DNS, though IPv6 adoption has matured and many issues described have been addressed or worked around in modern implementations.

sections.title: IPv6 in DNS Basics
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses are published in DNS using AAAA records in the forward zone and PTR records in the ip6.arpa tree for reverse lookups. Despite this, DNS remains transport-independent: AAAA records can be queried over IPv4 networks, and A records over IPv6 networks. DNS servers must not filter answers based on whether the query came over IPv4 or IPv6 transport.

To avoid fragmenting the DNS namespace into parts visible only via IPv4 or IPv6, every authoritative DNS zone should have at least one IPv4-enabled server, and recursive resolvers should be IPv4-enabled or dual-stack. This ensures the entire DNS remains reachable regardless of the transport protocol available to the client.
sections.eli5: IPv6 addresses go into a special section of the phone book, but you can ask about them using either old or new addresses. The phone book should always have at least one entry reachable the old way, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Special IPv6 Address Types
sections.content:
IPv6 includes several special address types that need careful DNS handling. Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) should never be published in DNS because they only work on a single network link, not the internet. Temporary addresses, which rotate for privacy, should not be in DNS either because publishing them would defeat their purpose.

6to4 addresses (2002:V4ADDR::/48) derived from public IPv4 addresses present a special challenge. Reverse DNS for 6to4 requires autonomous delegation systems, which introduces scalability concerns. Teredo addresses should not be placed in reverse DNS at all because they depend on temporary NAT mappings. Other transition mechanisms may need custom DNS solutions depending on how they encode addresses.
sections.eli5: Some new address types are local-only and should not be in the phone book. Others are temporary and keeping them there breaks their privacy feature. A few transition technologies need special workarounds.

sections.title: Known Implementation Problems
sections.content:
Several DNS servers and load-balancers have observed bugs that cause serious problems with IPv6 deployments. Some implementations silently drop queries for unknown record types instead of returning a proper negative response. This is catastrophic for IPv6 because applications typically query AAAA records first and then A records in sequence. When a broken server silently drops the AAAA query, the application times out waiting for a response, incurring significant delays or appearing to hang entirely.

The impact on IPv6 adoption has been severe enough that some organizations have disabled IPv6 support to work around these broken servers. The proper solution is to fix or retire the buggy implementations, but that is unlikely to happen quickly. Some mitigations include performing lookups in parallel (querying for A records without waiting for a full AAAA timeout) or reducing timeout values, but these remain to be standardized.
sections.eli5: Some broken phone books don't answer when you ask about new addresses; they just ignore you instead of saying 'not found.' This makes looking things up painfully slow.

sections.title: Service Provisioning and DNS Records
sections.content:
Rather than publishing IPv6 addresses on node hostnames, organizations should create separate service names (e.g., 'smtp.example.com' instead of 'server.example.com'). This allows flexibility: different services can migrate at different paces, have different TTL values, and be tested independently.

When deciding whether to publish IPv6 addresses for a service, do not add AAAA records until all three conditions are met: the IPv6 address is assigned to the interface, it is configured on the interface, and the interface has connectivity to the IPv6 infrastructure. Publishing AAAA records for services that are not yet fully IPv6-capable causes clients to attempt IPv6 connections that will fail, degrading performance.

One strategy is to use separate names like 'service.ipv6.example.com' during a pilot phase, then move to the same service name once confidence is high. TTL values require special attention: when A and AAAA records have different TTLs, caching systems may serve incomplete data during the TTL mismatch window, potentially causing reachability problems.
sections.eli5: Test IPv6 services with different names first to avoid slowing down regular users. Only list an address in the phone book when the service truly works there. When old and new addresses have different expiration times, keep them in sync to avoid strange problems.

sections.title: DNS Resolver Configuration
sections.content:
When IPv6 is enabled on a client, the system library's getaddrinfo() function may begin querying for AAAA records even when IPv6 connectivity does not exist. This creates three scenarios: the library queries IPv6 records even when IPv6 is disabled (always wasteful), it queries when IPv6 is enabled but not yet connected (still wasteful), or it queries only when meaningful IPv6 connectivity is present (ideal).

The most problematic case is when clients have only link-local IPv6 addresses (automatically generated for link-local communication) but no global IPv6 addresses. Applications should be able to detect this situation and avoid issuing AAAA queries. In addition, address selection may prefer AAAA records even when there is no IPv6 connectivity, causing long protocol timeouts instead of quick fallback to IPv4.

Resolvers need to know how to find DNS servers. DHCPv6 provides a mechanism to discover recursive DNS resolvers, though alternatives are still being explored for IPv6-only networks. Recursive resolvers themselves should support IPv4 or be dual-stack so they can reach all authoritative servers, even IPv4-only ones.
sections.eli5: When you turn on IPv6, don't immediately start asking about IPv6 addresses; check that you can actually reach IPv6 first, or you will get slow hangs. Clients need a way to find DNS servers on IPv6 networks.

sections.title: Updating Forward and Reverse DNS
sections.content:
Updating forward DNS (name-to-address mappings) is more straightforward than reverse DNS because the updater typically owns the DNS name and can establish a security relationship with it. Both manual updates and dynamic DNS (DDNS) are options, though dynamic DNS introduces additional complexity.

Reverse DNS updates are more challenging. For manual updates, an organization must manage the reverse delegation for its address space. For dynamic DNS, integration with address autoconfiguration methods (like stateless address autoconfiguration or DHCP) introduces operational complexity because IPv6 addresses can change more frequently than in IPv4 networks.

Transition mechanisms like 6to4 present special challenges: they generate addresses from IPv4 address information, making automated reverse DNS delegation possible but complex. The applicability of reverse DNS itself varies by use case and must be considered before investing in complex update mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Updating the phone book to map names to addresses is straightforward. Updating the reverse phone book (address to name) is harder, especially with IPv6 because addresses change more often.
